title: Epoxy Resin Systems: Protect Your Skin and Lungs
summary: Epoxies can cause skin rashes and allergies, asthma, and lung problems. Use ventilation, the right PPE, and good hygiene every time you mix, apply, or spray them.
talking_points: Epoxy resin systems are strong, durable coatings and adhesives used in many trades, including protective coatings on steel structures. They are dangerous on your skin and if you breathe vapors, mists, or particles.

Health effects include painful or itchy skin rashes, allergy (sensitization), asthma, lung inflammation, and lower lung function. Some chemicals may also affect hormones. See a doctor if you have symptoms.
Use ventilation. Local exhaust, like dust collectors on power tools, captures contaminants at the source. Fans or natural air movement help in enclosed or covered spaces.
Wear a long-sleeved shirt, polyethylene or polypropylene coveralls, and eye protection.
Wear thick nitrile or butyl rubber gloves. Never use cotton or latex gloves because they can hold the chemicals against your skin.

Respirators: a NIOSH-approved powered air-purifying respirator with particulate filter and organic vapor cartridge when spraying in enclosed spaces, and a half facepiece with organic vapor cartridge for mixing and roller or brush work. Keep 10 feet or more from workers using epoxy products, or wear a respirator if you work close by.
Wash with pH neutral soap and warm water before and after gloves and after any splash. Clean tools and reusable gloves after each use, and bag dirty clothes to wash separately.

Change into clean clothes before you leave, shower when you get home, keep work and storage areas clean, and keep containers tightly covered. Your employer must train you and give you safety data sheets and PPE.
site_hazards_to_check: Spraying or mixing epoxy in an enclosed or covered space with poor air movement
Workers wearing cotton or latex gloves
Missing coveralls, eye protection, or respirators
No handwashing station near the work
Other workers within 10 feet of epoxy application without a respirator
discussion_questions: What gloves and respirator do we need for this epoxy job?
Where can we wash up during and after the work?
Has anyone had a rash or breathing trouble from epoxies, and what did they do?
